=== Google and Lancium Comments to 58481 PFP.pdf ===
                                     PROJECT NO. 58481

  LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION §                          PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
  STANDARDS                  §                                   OF TEXAS
                             §

 GOOGLE AND LANCIUM JOINT COMMENTS TO STAFF PROPOSED PROPOSAL
                        FOR PUBLICATION


Introduction:
Google LLC and Lancium LLC (herein referred to as Joint Commenters) appreciate the
Commission’s effort to implement PURA §37.0561 and to address concerns about stranded
infrastructure risk. We also recognize that Staff is primarily defining the intermediate agreement
and interconnection agreement, while leaving study process details to ERCOT’s evolving large
load and batch study frameworks. However, those ERCOT study processes are still under
development and lack clear, final structure. Approving the Proposal For Publication (PFP) now
creates misalignment risk between Commission rules, ERCOT study processes, and actual
interconnection timelines.

As written, the draft PFP requires large, upfront, and non-refundable financial commitments
without providing clear study outcomes, defined interconnection timelines, or a predictable path
to energization. This sequencing shifts significant risk onto customers before system feasibility
and deliverability are known. As a result, the proposal may discourage credible, financeable
projects while disconnecting cost allocation from cost causation principles.



Joint Commenters share primary concerns around:
   ●​ Discouraging credible, financeable projects from investing and operating in Texas
      due to high uncertainty and risk exposure;

   ●​ Moving away from cost causation principles by assigning arbitrary standardized
      front-loaded costs that don’t necessarily reflect actual system impacts;

   ●​ Pancaking of security costs by requiring multiple forms of security that are not
      reflective of project development risks; and

   ●​ Requiring major financial commitments without a clear and predictable line of sight to
      energization or grid service




                                                1
 Joint Commenters are supportive of policies that:
  ●​ Deter speculative requests while allowing viable projects to advance;

  ●​ Maintain cost causation principles and allocate costs consistent with PURA and
     traditional regulatory practice;

  ●​ Efficient securitization by aligning financial commitments with project development
     risk;

  ●​ Use staged and proportionate financial commitments tied to project readiness and
     system feasibility;

  ●​ Establish a clear, phased interconnection process with defined milestones from
     request through energization; and

  ●​ Ensure large load customers fund direct interconnection costs without shifting
     costs to other ratepayers.



Joint Commenters support the following policy changes to the PFP:
  ●​ Require an early Transmission Service Provider (TSP) facilities study prior to
     major financial commitments.​
     A facilities-level assessment should be conducted early to establish technical feasibility
     and provide an initial estimate of customer-specific interconnection costs before large
     non-refundable or staged financial obligations are triggered.

  ●​ Make intermediate-stage financial security fully refundable after cost recovery.​
     Financial security posted at the intermediate agreement stage should be used only to
     cover actual, prudently-incurred study, engineering, and procurement costs. If a load
     reduces or withdraws its project, any remaining balance after cost recovery should be
     returned to the customer. Retaining 80% of the remaining funds is misaligned with cost
     causation principles and effectively operates as a penalty rather than a mechanism for
     recovering actual interconnection-related costs.

  ●​ Incorporate an early screening study within a batch study framework.​
     Joint Commenters recommend establishing a formal screening study as an initial step in
     the interconnection process. Loads evaluated in parallel within the batch framework
     would better reflect cumulative system impacts and yield more realistic and actionable
     results. After this step, developers would have clearer visibility into upgrade needs,
     available capacity, and likely energization timelines. The Commission should tie
     non-refundable financial commitments to the completion of this screening stage, when
     customers are better informed about project feasibility and interconnection timelines.



                                              2
    ●​ Limit non-refundable charges to CIAC and eliminate the separate non-refundable
      interconnection fee.​
      Current practice already requires customers to pay 100% of direct interconnection costs
      tied to actual facilities built to serve the load. A flat $100,000/MW non-refundable
      interconnection fee is not clearly tied to system impact and may result in over-collection
      beyond true interconnection costs. Joint Commenters have previously supported a
      minimum demand charge to guarantee a baseline of revenues over a fixed period of time
      once the load is energized, categorically derisking at least some of the investment and
      likely not necessitating significant operational security.

   ●​ Align financial commitment requirements with study results and system
      readiness.​
      Large financial obligations should not be imposed before system feasibility and
      deliverability are known. Financial commitments should be staged and informed by study
      outcomes, identified upgrades, and transmission planning timelines.

   ●​ Provide flexibility for delays and uncertainties outside the customer’s control​
      The rule should distinguish between customer-driven delays versus delays caused by
      transmission constraints, study scope changes, ERCOT processes, or planning timelines
      to avoid penalizing viable projects for circumstances outside their control. .



Outstanding Questions and Implementation Clarifications:
In addition to the policy refinements above, Joint Commenters respectfully request clarification
on several key implementation issues:

   ●​ Interaction between CIAC and financial security requirements​
      Clarify whether CIAC payments are separate from, or in addition to, financial security
      postings for equipment, services, and system upgrades, and whether these obligations
      are intended to stack. Joint Commenters support implementing the same financial
      commitment criteria in the 2026 RTP, adopted in 58480:

           ○​ “Posting of security in the amount of $100,000 per MW of contracted peak
              demand;

           ○​ “Posting of financial security to the DSP or TSP in an amount equal to the DSP
              and TSP’s expected costs for equipment with a lead time of at least six months
              and services necessary to interconnect the large load; or

           ○​ “Payment of contribution in aid of construction (CIAC) in an amount that is equal
              to the DSP and TSP’s expected costs to interconnect the large load customer
              that are directly attributable to interconnecting the large load customer.”



                                                3
    ●​ Whether financial security requirements are cumulative across phases​
      The rule requires $100,000/MW financial security at the intermediate agreement stage
      and an additional $100,000/MW non-refundable interconnection fee at the
      interconnection agreement stage. Clarification is needed on whether this effectively
      results in $200,000/MW or whether prior postings are credited forward. Joint
      Commenters oppose security pancaking and support limiting refundability of securities
      as the interconnection process progresses.

   ●​ Application of requirements where system upgrades are minimal or not required​
      Clarify how CIAC and financial security apply to behind-the-meter loads, co-located
      generation, or configurations that do not trigger significant system upgrades.

   ●​ Retroactive applicability and impacts on existing projects​
      Provide guidance on whether the rule is proposed to apply to projects already in the
      study or interconnection process and how prior investments will be treated. Joint
      Commenters do not support retroactive applicability, especially for projects with signed
      interconnection agreements that have already paid applicable security and/or CIAC.

   ●​ Practical impacts of compressed commitment timelines​
      The 30-day window to execute an interconnection agreement may not align with
      financing, governance, and capital allocation cycles for large industrial projects, including
      critical industries such as manufacturing and oil and gas.



Conclusion:
These comments reflect Joint Commenters’ initial thoughts on the draft PFP and are intended to
ensure alignment with core policy principles, including cost causation, regulatory clarity, and
predictable pathways to interconnection and grid service.

Joint Commenters appreciate Staff’s efforts to move quickly to implement PURA §37.0561 and
to provide structure around intermediate and interconnection agreements. However, given that
ERCOT’s large load and batch study processes are still evolving, additional refinement of the
PFP is important to avoid misalignment between Commission rules, study frameworks, and
real-world project development timelines.

Joint Commenters will provide more detailed and comprehensive comments in formal responses
to the PFP. We look forward to continued engagement with the Commission and Staff to ensure
the final rule supports reliability, protects ratepayers, and allows credible, financeable large load
projects to move forward in a predictable and transparent manner.




                                                 4
 ​

Respectfully submitted,

    Christopher Matos                    Evan Neel
    Energy Market Development Lead       Sr. Director, Regulatory and Power Services
    Google LLC                           Lancium LLC
